strengths: The paper addresses a timely and meaningful problem: reducing the sequential inference cost of continuous-token autoregressive image generators. Extending speculative decoding beyond discrete token distributions is a worthwhile Algorithms/General contribution for computer vision generation systems.

The proposed components are well motivated at a high level: density-ratio based acceptance for continuous outputs, denoising trajectory alignment to improve acceptance, token pre-filling for early AR mismatch, and acceptance-rejection sampling for the post-rejection distribution.

The empirical speedups are practically relevant in the evaluated setting, reaching up to 2.33x for MAR-H with MAR-B drafts at large batch sizes, while FID/IS remain close to the target MAR baseline on ImageNet 256 generation.

The ablations are useful: the paper separately studies trajectory alignment, pre-filling, draft length, CFG scale, temperature, and rejection sampling attempts, which helps explain when the method is effective.

The manuscript is mostly clear and includes supplementary proof sketches and implementation details. The method is training-free and uses off-the-shelf MAR checkpoints, which improves its practical appeal.
weaknesses: The central technical claim that the implemented procedure preserves the target output distribution is not fully convincing. The derivation treats the diffusion sampling trajectory density ratio as if it gives the marginal output density ratio p(x0)/q(x0), but for diffusion decoders the marginal generally involves integration over latent trajectories/noise. The trajectory-aligned calculation is a coupling of samplers, not obviously an exact density-ratio estimator for the generated token distribution. The correctness proof assumes exact p/q and therefore does not establish correctness of the approximation actually used.

The acceptance-rejection resampling step also depends on being able to sample from and evaluate the target distribution accurately. For continuous diffusion-token decoders, this can be costly and approximate; the paper states the overhead is negligible but gives limited analysis of how many target denoising passes are required and how this interacts with the reported wall-time speedups.

The experimental scope is narrow: all results are on MAR variants for ImageNet 256. There is no evaluation on other continuous autoregressive image models, text-to-image continuous AR models, higher resolutions, or non-ImageNet data, so generality remains uncertain.

The practical speedup is uneven. For batch size 1, speedups are often small, especially for MAR-L as target, and some configurations are near 1.0x. The strongest 2.33x result appears at batch size 256, which may not reflect common latency-sensitive generation use cases.

The quality evidence relies mainly on FID/IS and qualitative samples. Since the paper claims distribution preservation, stronger statistical comparisons, per-class degradation analysis, diversity metrics, or exact-seed comparisons would be valuable. Table 2 also omits key decoding settings such as draft length and pre-fill ratio, making the quality/speed tradeoff harder to interpret.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the code URL is blank, implementation details are somewhat high level, and several figures/tables are difficult to parse visually. More precise pseudocode for MAR-specific density evaluation, wall-time measurement, and rejection sampling would help.

The paper does not compare against potentially relevant acceleration baselines for image generation inference, even if no exact continuous speculative decoding baseline exists. Comparisons to simpler alternatives such as reduced diffusion steps, early exiting, lower precision, or using the draft model alone at matched compute would better contextualize the benefit.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant efficiency problem: accelerating continuous-valued autoregressive image generators such as MAR without retraining or architecture changes. Extending speculative decoding beyond discrete token distributions is a worthwhile direction for computer vision generation systems.

The manuscript identifies several real obstacles in the continuous setting, including how to evaluate density ratios, how denoising trajectories differ between draft and target models, and how to sample after rejection from a modified continuous distribution.

The empirical section reports wall-clock measurements across batch sizes, draft lengths, and MAR model pairs, plus FID/IS comparisons on ImageNet 256x256. The reported best-case speedup of 2.33x for MAR-H with MAR-B at large batch size is potentially useful if the method is correct.

Ablations for trajectory alignment, pre-filling, draft length, CFG scale, temperature, and rejection-sampling retries are helpful and suggest the authors made a serious attempt to understand acceptance behavior.
weaknesses: The core theoretical justification is not convincing. Speculative decoding requires the acceptance ratio p(x)/q(x) for the same proposed sample x under the target and draft output distributions. The paper instead appears to use a single denoising trajectory or aligned random noise path to approximate this ratio. For diffusion-generated continuous tokens, the marginal density of x0 generally requires integrating over latent trajectories/noise paths; a path-density ratio is not automatically a valid final-sample density ratio. This undermines the central claim of preserving the target distribution.

The denoising trajectory alignment changes the coupling between draft and target sampling and is argued mainly through simplification of Gaussian terms. The derivation seems to compare different intermediate states xp_t and xq_t and relies on shared epsilon values, but this does not establish that the resulting acceptance rule is exact for the target marginal distribution. Thus the method may be heuristic while being presented as theoretically lossless.

The acceptance-rejection resampling argument is also under-specified. Sampling from the target model distribution p(x) is itself a full denoising process, and the acceptance probability again uses the questionable density approximation. The claim that the integral-free bound preserves correctness follows algebraically only if the true p(x) and q(x) are available, which the paper has not established.

The experiments do not adequately validate the strongest claim, namely maintaining the original output distribution. FID and IS on 50k ImageNet samples are coarse aggregate metrics and can miss distributional differences; there are no stronger two-sample tests, likelihood checks, precision/recall metrics, per-class analyses, or comparisons of exact versus approximate acceptance behavior in a controlled setting where the true continuous densities are known.

The practical impact is narrower than claimed. The headline 2.33x speedup occurs only for MAR-H/MAR-B at batch size 256; single-image generation speedups are much smaller, and MAR-L/MAR-B reaches only about 1.18x at best for batch size 1. For several settings the speedup is near 1.0, so the benefit is highly conditional on batching and model-pair choice.

The empirical scope is limited to MAR on ImageNet 256x256. The paper does not test other continuous-token AR models such as GIVT, DisCo-Diff, DART-like systems, text-to-image settings, higher resolutions, or larger target models. The claim that gains will improve for 7B/13B-scale models is speculative.

The quality evaluation is incomplete for an acceleration paper. The main FID/IS table does not clearly report the draft length, pre-fill ratio, batch setting, or speed-quality tradeoff corresponding to each number, making it hard to assess whether the most accelerated settings preserve quality.

Important baselines are missing. The paper does not compare against simpler acceleration strategies, relaxed speculative decoding variants adapted heuristically, caching/parallelization baselines, or a naive draft-and-repair method with similar compute. This makes it difficult to isolate the value of the proposed density-ratio machinery.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. The authors say code will be available but provide no repository, and several implementation details that affect correctness and runtime are unclear, including how variance determinants are computed in high-dimensional token space, how numerical underflow is handled, and how the acceptance-rejection loop is bounded in practice.

The writing is generally understandable, but some equations contain notation errors or formatting artifacts, and the exposition repeatedly states exact distribution preservation more strongly than the derivation and evidence justify. Given the centrality of this claim, the paper needs a much more rigorous and careful treatment.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely bottleneck: inference acceleration for continuous-token autoregressive image generators. Extending speculative decoding beyond discrete token distributions is a meaningful Algorithms/General contribution for computer vision generation models.

The proposed method is conceptually well motivated: it identifies the key obstacles in the continuous setting, including density-ratio estimation, low draft-target consistency, and sampling from the post-rejection modified distribution. The denoising trajectory alignment, target-token pre-filling, and acceptance-rejection resampling form a coherent framework.

The empirical results are promising. On MAR ImageNet 256x256 generation, the method reports up to 2.33x wall-clock speedup while maintaining similar FID and IS, and the paper includes useful ablations for draft length, trajectory alignment, pre-filling ratio, CFG scale, temperature, and rejection-sampling trial counts.

The method is training-free and uses off-the-shelf MAR checkpoints, which strengthens practical relevance and reproducibility in principle. The ablations show that the proposed alignment substantially improves acceptance rate compared with unaligned denoising trajectories.
weaknesses: The theoretical exactness claim is not fully convincing as written. Speculative decoding requires the density ratio of the final continuous token distribution, but the paper appears to compute a ratio along constructed denoising trajectories. For diffusion-style generation, the marginal density of x0 generally involves integrating over latent trajectories, so the product of conditional densities along one aligned path may not equal the true token marginal density. The correctness proof assumes access to true p(x) and q(x), but does not fully justify that the implemented estimator is exactly that quantity.

The evaluation scope is limited to MAR on ImageNet 256x256 with model sizes up to 943M. This is a reasonable first demonstration, but the paper's broader claim about continuous-valued visual AR models would be stronger with experiments on another continuous AR model or higher-resolution/text-conditioned generation.

The practical speedups are uneven: gains are strongest at large batch sizes, while batch size 1 speedups are often modest and sometimes near 1.0x. Since image generation is often latency-sensitive, the paper should more clearly separate throughput-oriented gains from single-sample latency gains.

The paper relies mainly on FID and IS to support distribution preservation. Given the central claim of maintaining the target output distribution, stronger evidence such as paired/random-seed analyses, precision/recall or density/coverage metrics, more extensive human/visual comparison, or direct diagnostics of acceptance-ratio correctness would improve confidence.

Some implementation and reproducibility details remain under-specified. The manuscript says code will be available but provides no link, and the exact accounting of rejection-resampling cost, parallel verification scheduling, and memory overhead is not fully transparent.

There are clarity issues in the math and writing, including apparent sign/notation problems in the Gaussian density derivation and occasional imprecise phrasing. These do not invalidate the empirical contribution, but they matter because the paper leans heavily on theoretical correctness.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: accelerating continuous visual autoregressive generation, where standard discrete speculative decoding does not directly apply. The framing around continuous output densities, rejection sampling for the residual distribution, and draft-target trajectory alignment is original and relevant to ECCV.

The proposed method is appealingly practical: it is training-free, requires no architectural changes, and is demonstrated on multiple continuous visual AR backbones, including MAR, xAR, and Harmon, with reported wall-clock speedups often around or above 2x at larger batch sizes.

The manuscript includes useful ablations on draft length, trajectory alignment, pre-filling ratio, temperature, CFG scale, and rejection-sampling overhead. The comparison to masked generation helps clarify the quality-speed tradeoff relative to a plausible acceleration alternative.
The authors acknowledge an important limitation: speedup is constrained by the draft/target runtime ratio, and gains are modest when the draft model is not much cheaper or batch size is small.
weaknesses: The theoretical correctness claim is not fully convincing. The proof assumes access to exact p(x)/q(x) and exact sampling from the modified distribution, but the implementation appears to use a product of conditional densities along a sampled diffusion trajectory as if it were the marginal output density. For diffusion-based generators, the marginal likelihood of x0 generally involves integration over latent paths, so the acceptance ratio used may not be the true target/draft density ratio. This weakens the central claim that the method preserves the original target distribution.

Denoising trajectory alignment changes or couples the stochastic paths used by draft and target models. The paper argues that sharing noise reduces expected trajectory distance, but it does not rigorously show that the resulting verification ratio remains the correct density ratio for the target output distribution. The distribution-preservation proof in Appendix A.3 is generic speculative decoding algebra and does not address this approximation gap.

Experimental evidence for distribution preservation is incomplete. FID/IS are reported mainly for MAR, while xAR and Harmon are used mostly for speed measurements. For Harmon text-to-image generation, there is no clear quantitative quality evaluation such as FID, CLIPScore, human preference, or prompt-alignment metrics, despite claims of maintaining quality across models and resolutions.

The reported speedups are less broadly strong than the headline suggests. At batch size 1, some settings obtain only about 1.1x to 1.6x speedup, and the best gains rely on large batch sizes where parallel verification is more favorable. The paper should state this dependency more prominently and analyze latency-sensitive single-sample generation more carefully.

The experimental comparisons are limited. Since the method is positioned as an inference accelerator, stronger baselines would be helpful, including simpler parallel/masked decoding variants, reduced diffusion-step sampling, distillation or smaller-model sampling, and model-specific batching optimizations under matched quality.

Reproducibility and presentation need improvement. The abstract says code is available but the URL is missing. Some implementation details are underspecified, including exact runtime measurement protocol, prompt sets for Harmon, prefill selection, memory usage, and how acceptance ratios are numerically stabilized in high-dimensional token spaces. The manuscript also contains many language and formatting issues that obscure technical points.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and relevant efficiency problem: accelerating continuous visual autoregressive image generators without retraining or changing model architectures. Extending speculative decoding beyond discrete token distributions is an interesting direction for ECCV.

The method is evaluated on several continuous visual AR backbones, including MAR, xAR, and Harmon, and reports nontrivial wall-clock speedups, especially at larger batch sizes. The ablations on draft length, trajectory alignment, pre-filling, temperature, CFG, and rejection-sampling overhead are useful.

The manuscript identifies real practical obstacles for continuous speculative decoding, namely low acceptance rates and resampling from the modified distribution, and attempts to connect algorithm design with theoretical distribution preservation.
weaknesses: The main theoretical foundation appears unsound or at least insufficiently justified. The paper treats the product of conditional diffusion transition densities along a sampled denoising trajectory as the density of the final token, but the marginal probability of the generated continuous token generally requires integrating over latent trajectories. This is central because the speculative acceptance ratio must use the true target/draft output densities, not a path-dependent surrogate.

The denoising trajectory alignment proof only shows that coupling the Gaussian noise variables can reduce expected sample distance under a particular reparameterization. It does not establish that the target and draft output distributions become closer in the sense required for valid speculative decoding, nor that the resulting acceptance ratio preserves the target distribution. The claimed lossless distribution preservation therefore remains unconvincing.

Several derivations are mathematically sloppy or questionable, including sign errors in Gaussian density expressions, unclear handling of covariance determinants, assumptions such as shared initial noise and fixed AR context, and an acceptance-rejection sampler whose proposal and threshold rely on the same questionable density simplification. These are not minor presentation issues because they support the paper's core correctness claim.

The experimental evidence does not adequately validate the strongest claims. Distribution preservation is assessed mainly with FID/IS and visual examples, which are too weak to support a lossless or exact target-distribution claim. There is no direct statistical test of equivalence to the target sampler, no analysis of bias introduced by the approximate acceptance ratio, and no comparison on downstream or perceptual diversity metrics beyond limited aggregate scores.

Quality preservation results are incomplete across the claimed scope. Detailed FID/IS comparisons are shown only for MAR, while xAR and Harmon are mainly used for speed tables. For a method claimed to integrate seamlessly into multiple continuous visual AR models, the quality and failure-mode evaluation should be broader.

The practical speedup case is mixed. The strongest speedups occur at large batch sizes, while batch-size-1 latency gains are often modest; the appendix notes that draft and target models have a relatively high runtime ratio. This limits the impact for interactive generation, yet the main text emphasizes over 2x acceleration without sufficiently qualifying the batching dependence.

The code availability statement is blank, which harms reproducibility. Key implementation details, especially how path likelihoods, aligned noise, target verification, and rejection sampling are computed in real model code, are essential for assessing correctness.

The paper has clarity and presentation issues: several figures/tables appear poorly rendered in extraction, notation is overloaded, and the algorithm description is hard to reconcile with the mathematical claims. These problems make it difficult to verify the method independently.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important efficiency problem for continuous visual autoregressive generation, where standard discrete speculative decoding does not directly apply. Extending speculative decoding to continuous token distributions is a natural but nontrivial contribution with clear relevance to computer vision generation models.

The method is technically substantive: it identifies two concrete obstacles, low acceptance from draft/target distribution mismatch and sampling from the modified continuous distribution, and proposes denoising trajectory alignment, token pre-filling, and acceptance-rejection sampling with a computable threshold.

The empirical evidence is fairly broad for this niche: experiments cover MAR, xAR, and Harmon, with 256 and 512 resolution settings, multiple draft lengths, and batch sizes. Reported wall-time speedups are meaningful, reaching about 2.3x on MAR, 2.7x on xAR, and 2.5x on Harmon in favorable settings.

Generation quality appears well preserved on MAR, with FID/IS close to the target model under both unconditional and CFG settings, and the qualitative comparisons support the claim that acceleration does not obviously degrade samples.

The ablations are useful and directly tied to the proposed components. In particular, denoising trajectory alignment substantially improves acceptance rate and reduces draft-target token distance, while the paper also studies pre-filling, draft length, temperature, CFG, rejection-sampling cost, and masked-generation alternatives.
The contribution is training-free and integrates with off-the-shelf continuous AR models, which increases practical appeal and lowers the adoption barrier.
weaknesses: The theoretical presentation is promising but not fully airtight. The correctness proof establishes the usual continuous speculative decoding distributional identity under ideal densities, but the implemented procedure relies on denoising trajectory alignment and simplified likelihood ratios along sampled diffusion trajectories. The paper should more carefully justify that these approximations/couplings still preserve the exact target distribution, or explicitly frame the method as approximate where applicable.

The strongest speedups appear at larger batch sizes; batch size 1 speedups are more modest, especially for MAR. This limits the claim of broadly over-2x acceleration for latency-sensitive single-sample generation, and the paper could discuss this more prominently in the main results.

Quality evaluation is uneven across models. FID/IS preservation is reported mainly for MAR, while xAR and Harmon results focus on speed and acceptance. For a general method across continuous AR models, comparable quality metrics for all evaluated backbones and resolutions would strengthen the evidence.

Comparisons to existing acceleration methods are limited. The paper includes a masked-generation comparison, but there is little direct comparison to recent visual speculative decoding/Jacobi-style methods where applicable, or to simpler engineering baselines such as reducing diffusion steps, using DDIM fewer steps, or model-size tradeoffs at matched wall time and quality.

Some experimental choices need clearer justification. For xAR, the model is changed to predict next token at each position rather than its original next-cell setup; it is not fully clear how this affects baseline speed/quality or whether the reported speedups reflect the most natural xAR usage.

Reproducibility is somewhat weakened by missing or incomplete details: the abstract says code is available but no link is provided, several implementation specifics are relegated to the appendix, and the exact timing protocol, warmup, variance of wall-time measurements, and memory constraints are not fully characterized.

The writing and formatting have several rough edges, including typos, awkward phrases, and some hard-to-read extracted/rendered math/figure text. These do not undermine the main contribution, but they reduce clarity for a theory-heavy method.
